name: Electrolytes & Acid–Base
sub: ABG interpretation, anion gap, sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium

cards.q: Give Winter's formula and its use.
cards.a: Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 (± 2). If the measured PaCO₂ is higher, there is an additional respiratory acidosis; lower means a concurrent respiratory alkalosis.

cards.q: How do you calculate the anion gap and what causes a raised gap?
cards.a: AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). Raised in GOLDMARK: Glycols, Oxoproline, L-lactate, D-lactate, Methanol, Aspirin, Renal failure, Ketoacidosis.

cards.q: How do you interpret the delta ratio?
cards.a: ΔAG ÷ ΔHCO₃⁻: 1–2 indicates a pure high-gap acidosis; <1 suggests a concurrent normal-gap acidosis; >2 suggests concurrent metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: What are the main causes of a normal anion gap acidosis?
cards.a: Diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis, large-volume saline, acetazolamide, ureteric diversion. A positive urine anion gap suggests renal acidification failure.

cards.q: Outline the steps for emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia.
cards.a: Calcium gluconate 10% 10–30 mL IV; insulin (regular 10 units) with 25 g dextrose; salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised; bicarbonate if acidotic; loop diuretic if making urine; remove with binders or dialysis; stop potassium-raising drugs.

cards.q: What is the maximum rate of potassium replacement?
cards.a: Peripheral: up to 10 mmol/h; central line with cardiac monitoring: up to 20 mmol/h (concentrated solutions). Check and correct magnesium.

cards.q: What is the safe rate of correction of chronic hyponatraemia?
cards.a: No more than 8–10 mmol/L in any 24 hours (up to 8 in high-risk) to avoid osmotic demyelination, with close sodium checks every 2–4 hours.

cards.q: How do you treat severe symptomatic hyponatraemia?
cards.a: 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL IV over 20 minutes (or 100 mL boluses), repeated up to 2–3 times to raise sodium 4–6 mmol/L, then stop and reassess.

cards.q: Give the diagnostic criteria for SIADH.
cards.a: Hypotonic hyponatraemia, euvolaemia, urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg, urine sodium >30 mmol/L, normal thyroid, adrenal and renal function and no diuretic use.

cards.q: How do you calculate the free-water deficit in hypernatraemia?
cards.a: Free water deficit (L) = total body water × (Na⁺/140 − 1), where TBW is about 0.6 × weight in men and 0.5 × in women. Lower sodium by no more than about 10 mmol/L per day.

cards.q: How does diabetes insipidus present and how is it treated?
cards.a: Polyuria (>3 L/day) with dilute urine and hypernatraemia. Central DI: desmopressin 1–2 mcg IV or SC; nephrogenic: treat the cause (lithium, hypercalcaemia) and use thiazides and a low-sodium diet.

cards.x: In hyperglycaemia, measured sodium falls by about {{c1::1.6}} mmol/L for each {{c2::100}} mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) of glucose above normal.

cards.q: How do you treat symptomatic hypocalcaemia?
cards.a: IV calcium: 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate (about 90 mg elemental) over 10 minutes, or 10% calcium chloride 10 mL (about 270 mg elemental) via a central line, followed by an infusion; check magnesium.

cards.q: How is severe hypercalcaemia treated?
cards.a: Isotonic saline hydration (4–6 L/day), calcitonin for rapid effect, a bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid 4 mg, loop diuretics after volume restoration, steroids in granulomatous or lymphoid disease, and dialysis in refractory cases.

cards.q: Which dose of magnesium treats hypomagnesaemia and torsades?
cards.a: Magnesium sulphate 2 g (8 mmol) IV over 10–20 minutes for torsades or severe deficiency, then 4–8 mmol/hour as an infusion in symptomatic or refractory hypomagnesaemia.

cards.q: What is refeeding syndrome and how do you prevent it?
cards.a: Fluid and electrolyte shifts (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia) with thiamine deficiency on re-introduction of feeding. Give thiamine before feeding, start slowly (10–20 kcal/kg/day) and monitor electrolytes daily.

cards.q: When is sodium bicarbonate indicated in metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: In severe acidaemia (pH <7.2) with AKI stage 2–3 (BICAR-ICU); SSC suggests against it in lactic acidosis with pH ≥7.2. Also used for TCA toxicity, hyperkalaemia and certain poisonings.

cards.q: What are the typical compensations for metabolic alkalosis?
cards.a: PaCO₂ rises about 0.7 mmHg for each 1 mmol/L rise in HCO₃⁻. Chloride-responsive alkalosis has urine chloride <20 mmol/L (vomiting, diuretics); chloride-resistant has urine chloride >20 mmol/L (hyperaldosteronism, Bartter or Gitelman).

cards.q: List causes of hypokalaemia in ICU.
cards.a: Diuretics, GI loss, insulin, beta-agonists, refeeding, alkalosis, hypomagnesaemia, and amphotericin B.

cards.q: What are normal serum electrolyte ranges?
cards.a: Sodium 135–145 mmol/L, potassium 3.5–5.0 mmol/L, ionised calcium 1.1–1.3 mmol/L, magnesium 0.7–1.0 mmol/L, phosphate 0.8–1.5 mmol/L.

cards.q: ABG: pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 28 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L; Na⁺ 140, Cl⁻ 100 mmol/L. What is the diagnosis?
o: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Normal anion gap acidosis with respiratory alkalosis
cards.e: AG = 140 − (100 + 12) = 28. Winter's expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × 12 + 8 = 26 ± 2; the measured 28 is within range, so compensation is appropriate.

cards.q: A 45-year-old with Na⁺ 108 mmol/L has seizures. What is the best initial therapy?
o: 3% saline bolus (100–150 mL) to raise sodium by 4–6 mmol/L
cards.e: Symptomatic severe hyponatraemia needs hypertonic saline for a quick rise of 4–6 mmol/L to reverse cerebral oedema; avoid overcorrection.

cards.q: What distinguishes pseudohyponatraemia?
cards.a: Normal measured osmolality with low sodium caused by marked hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia in older flame photometry; direct ion-selective electrodes avoid this error.
